explain: A responsibility is a posterior probability of membership, computed from the weighted densities of all components. It is not a geometric fraction, converged EM keeps soft values wherever components overlap, and an outlier far from everything can still get a responsibility near 1 for the widest component.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram
question: Why is Ward linkage described as similar to k-means?
options: It uses k-means++ seeding to choose the first merge
Each merge is the one that adds the least within-cluster sum of squares, which is the k-means objective, optimised greedily from the bottom up
It computes the same Voronoi cells as k-means at every height
It runs Lloyd's algorithm after every merge
explain: Ward's merge cost is the increase in SSE, the same inertia k-means minimises, so each cut is a greedy attempt at the k-means optimum. Here it found the optimum for k = 2 and k = 3, but greedy merges are never undone, so in general it can do worse than k-means with good seeding.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
question: A dashboard query computes AVG(amount) and COUNT(*) grouped by region over 500 million rows of a 40-column table. What is the main reason a columnar layout helps?
options: It reads only the 2 needed columns instead of all 40, cutting bytes scanned roughly 20x
Column stores keep an index on every column, so the scan becomes index lookups
Each row is stored contiguously, so the CPU prefetcher works better
Columnar files are always smaller because they skip null values
explain: The query touches region and amount only. A column layout lets the scan skip the other 38 columns entirely, so it moves about 2/40 of the bytes (less after compression). No per-column index is needed; the win is the layout itself.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
question: After Select, a vector of 1024 rows has a selection vector of length 900. The next primitive computes price x quantity. Which is the usual behavior?
options: It loops over the 900 positions in the selection vector and writes results at those same positions
It first copies the 900 rows into new contiguous vectors, then computes
It computes all 1024 rows and Select is re-applied afterwards
It switches to tuple-at-a-time for the selected rows
explain: X100 primitives accept an optional selection vector and compute only for those positions, writing at the same positions, because leaving the child's vectors intact is usually cheaper than copying the selected data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
question: Why can inlining make a program slower even though it removes call instructions?
options: Inlined code cannot be vectorized
It always disables constant folding
Inlined functions run at -O0
Duplicated bodies grow the code and can cause instruction-cache misses
explain: Every call site gets its own copy. For large functions with many call sites, the bigger hot path may no longer fit in the instruction cache, and those misses can cost more than the calls saved. Compilers use size budgets for this reason.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
question: Why does monolithic LTO hurt the edit-compile-test loop on a large project?
options: Any edit forces re-optimizing the single merged module of the whole program
It disables -O2
It cannot run on multicore machines at all
It requires profile data
explain: Monolithic LTO merges every module into one and optimizes it as a unit, so a one-line change redoes the expensive whole-program step. ThinLTO's cache re-runs only the backends whose inputs changed.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: The harness follows the docs' helper and sends a 1356x847 screenshot of the 2560x1600 display. The model asks to click (412, 236). Where should the harness click?
options: (824, 472), because the display is twice the 1280x800 size
(412, 236), because the API rescales coordinates automatically
(218, 125), multiplying by the scale factor 0.5299
explain: The factor is display over screenshot: 2560/1356 = 1.8879 and 1600/847 = 1.8890, giving (778, 446). Multiplying by s goes the wrong direction, and 2.0 is only right for an exact 1280x800 screenshot. The API never rescales for you. The docs' own code divides by s instead, giving (778, 445): integer screenshot sizes make the two methods differ by a pixel.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
question: Your harness asks the user to confirm once per model turn before running the turn's actions. The model returns a batch: click Buy now, click Confirm order, screenshot. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: one confirmation per turn covers all actions in it
The confirmation should be skipped for screenshots, but the design is otherwise fine
A batch can complete an irreversible multistep action in one turn, so the check must run before each consequential block, with the user seeing what each will do
Batches containing purchases are rejected by the API
explain: The docs say that when you confirm consequential actions, you should make that check before each block runs, because a batch can complete a multistep action within one turn. A per-turn prompt shown before the screen changes cannot tell the user what the second click will commit to.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
question: Two threads each increment a different field of one struct, `a` at offset 0 and `b` at offset 4, with no locks. Does TSan report a race?
options: Yes, they share an 8-byte shadow cell
Yes, any unsynchronized access to the same struct is a race
No, their byte masks do not overlap, so they are different memory locations
Only if the struct is heap-allocated
explain: A data race needs the same memory location. TSan records which bytes each access touched and only compares accesses whose byte ranges overlap. (They may still suffer false sharing, a performance issue, not a correctness one.)

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Training: consistency distillation, consistency training, EMA
question: A CD run uses an Euler teacher with N = 18 and reaches near-zero training loss, but one-step samples are slightly too smooth (under-dispersed). What change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer at the same settings
Use a higher-order teacher solver (Heun) or more grid points N
Increase the EMA decay to 0.99999
Set c_out(eps) to 0.5
explain: Zero CD loss means the model copies the teacher's one-step solver error, which accumulates along the chain (15% in the toy with Euler, N = 18). Heun or larger N shrinks it (5.5% with Heun, 0.2% with Heun and N = 80). Training longer cannot fix a biased target, and c_out(eps) must stay 0.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
question: Which pair of guarantees can both be offered while staying sticky available during a network partition?
options: Linearizability and sequential consistency
Sequential consistency and causal consistency
Causal consistency and read your writes
Linearizability and read your writes
explain: Per Jepsen and Bailis et al., causal consistency, PRAM (pipelined RAM, defined in lesson 5) and read your writes are sticky available. Sequential consistency and linearizability cannot be totally or sticky available: during a partition some nodes must refuse or block.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: The hash ring: each key goes to the next node clockwise
question: A ring has 9 equal arcs, one token per node, holding 900,000 keys. You add a 10th node whose single token splits one arc exactly in half. How many keys move, and is the result balanced?
options: 90,000, and every node now holds 90,000
50,000, all taken from one neighbour, so the new node and that neighbour hold 50,000 each while the others keep 100,000
810,000, because every key is rehashed
100,000, taken evenly from all nine nodes
explain: Each arc holds 900,000 / 9 = 100,000 keys. The new token takes half of one arc: 50,000 keys, all from a single neighbour. Movement is minimal, but the new node gets half a fair share and the eight untouched nodes stay at 100,000. One token per node cannot take load evenly from everyone; virtual nodes fix that.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
question: A recruiter types the free-text phrase `distributed systems` and also selects the facet location = New York. Where should each go?
options: Both in filter, for caching
Both in must, so both affect the score
The phrase in must (its text relevance should rank results), the location facet in filter
The phrase in filter, the location in should
explain: Text relevance is graded, so the phrase belongs in query context, where BM25 (the text relevance score from the ranking features course, built from how often the query terms occur, how rare they are, and field length) contributes to the score. A selected facet is a yes or no requirement on a structured field: filter context, no scoring work, and cacheable.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
question: After A=1 with forward checking, B, C and D all have domain {2,3}. Which variable does MRV with the degree tie-break choose?
options: C, because it comes first alphabetically after B
D, because it was assigned last in the plain search
B, because it constrains two unassigned variables (C and D)
Any of them; the degree heuristic only applies at the root
explain: MRV ties at 2 values each. The degree heuristic counts constraints to other unassigned variables: B has two (B,C and B,D), C and D have one each. Assigning B first fixes the most other domains, so B is picked.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
question: An attacker has code execution in a pod that runs as non-root, has no extra capabilities and no host mounts, but has the default service account token mounted and network access to the API server. What is the most realistic next step?
options: Use the mounted token to call the Kubernetes API with whatever rights that service account has
Escape to the host through the shared kernel immediately
Read other containers' memory through the cgroup
Nothing; non-root containers are fully isolated
explain: No fence was removed, so an escape needs a fresh kernel or runtime bug. The token is free: it is a credential sitting in the filesystem, and the API server is reachable. Its rights decide the blast radius, which is why RBAC and automount settings matter (lessons 8 and 9).

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
question: Which single setting gives a container control equivalent to root on the node without any kernel or runtime bug?
options: runAsNonRoot: true
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Mounting the container runtime's socket, such as /var/run/docker.sock
A memory limit of 64 MiB
explain: The runtime daemon runs as root and will start whatever container it is asked to, including one with the host filesystem mounted. Docker documents that even docker group membership is root-level access.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
question: You must stop one compromised user immediately. They are a member of system:masters. What works?
options: Delete their ClusterRoleBindings
Remove them from RBAC Roles
Add a deny rule for them
Revoke their credential (for example the client certificate) at the authentication layer, because system:masters bypasses RBAC
explain: system:masters skips RBAC, so bindings are irrelevant, and RBAC has no deny rules. The fix is at authentication. The authentication docs state Kubernetes does not support certificate revocation, so for a client certificate this can mean rotating the signing CA.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
question: Encryption at rest with KMS v2 is enabled. A developer has `list secrets` in namespace shop. What does encryption at rest change for them?
options: They now see ciphertext
Nothing: the API server decrypts on read, so authorized readers see plain values
List no longer returns values
They need the KMS key
explain: Encryption at rest protects etcd's stored data and backups. Anyone the API server authorizes still gets the decrypted value, which is why RBAC on Secrets is the main control.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
question: Which pair of controls together would have prevented both the Tesla and the Hildegard initial access?
options: Requiring authentication on every management interface (consoles, kubelets) and keeping them off the internet
Image scanning and signing
Resource limits and QoS classes
Encryption at rest and KMS
explain: Both started from a management interface that accepted unauthenticated requests from the internet. Authentication plus network exposure control closes that door; the other controls matter later in the chain.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement
question: A pod has one container with requests of cpu 200m and memory 256Mi, and limits of cpu 1 and memory 256Mi. What is its QoS class?
options: Guaranteed, because the memory request equals the memory limit
BestEffort, because the CPU is not pinned
Burstable, because the CPU request and limit differ
Guaranteed, because both requests are set
explain: Guaranteed requires request to equal limit for both CPU and memory, in every container. Memory matches here but CPU does not (200m against 1000m), so the pod is Burstable: evicted after BestEffort pods and before Guaranteed ones, and only while it is using more than its requests.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
question: Location is a multi-valued list currently holding [US]. The user says *also Canada*. What should the new value be?
options: [Canada]
null
dontcare
[US, Canada]
explain: With a multi-valued slot, *also* adds to the list. [Canada] would be the result of *Canada instead*. The schema has to declare the slot multi-valued for this to work at all.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: On a task, early-answering AOC is 0.02. What is the most accurate reading?
options: The CoT is 98% faithful
The model's answer is nearly always the same with or without the rest of its CoT, so the reasoning is mostly post-hoc
The model makes mistakes in 2% of its CoTs
Truncating the CoT almost always changes the answer
explain: AOC near 0 means the match curve sits near 100% from the start: the answer was set before the reasoning was read. That is evidence of post-hoc reasoning, not a faithfulness percentage. Option D describes a high AOC.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
question: In Baker et al. Table 1, the CoT monitor's joint recall is 95% vs 60% for the action-only monitor. What made the difference?
options: The CoT monitor was a stronger model than the action monitor
The CoT monitor saw the agent state its intent, which is more legible than a short code patch
The CoT monitor was trained on regex labels
The action monitor saw only half of the episodes
explain: Both monitors were the same prompted GPT-4o, and neither was trained. The only difference was input: the CoT monitor also read the reasoning, where the agent often said plainly what it planned to do.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: Your profile shows a 16 ms H2D copy that never overlaps with the kernel, even though you call cudaMemcpyAsync on a non-default stream. What is the most likely cause?
options: The stream was created without cudaStreamNonBlocking
The GPU has only one copy engine
The host buffer came from malloc, so the copy reverted to synchronous behaviour
The kernel and the copy touch the same device allocation
explain: A pageable source makes cudaMemcpyAsync revert to synchronous behaviour that "will not overlap with other work". The stream flag matters only for interaction with the legacy default stream, a single copy engine still overlaps one transfer with kernels, and sharing a device allocation across streams is a correctness problem, not an overlap blocker.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Two kernels at once: concurrency, stream priorities, comm overlap
question: In tensor-parallel decode you move each layer's all-reduce to a separate stream, but the profile shows no overlap at all. What is the most likely reason?
options: NCCL ignores the stream argument and always uses the default stream
The all-reduce must run on a lower-priority stream to overlap
All-reduces run on the copy engines, which are busy with H2D copies
The next layer's compute needs the all-reduce's result, so no independent work exists to run beside it; split the batch so one part's all-reduce overlaps another part's compute
explain: A separate stream only allows overlap of independent work. Every layer's compute depends on the previous all-reduce, so the dependency chain is serial. Splitting into nano-batches creates independent work: in the toy model, 32 layers drop from 44.80 ms to 32.20 ms. NCCL does honour its stream argument, and its collectives run as CUDA blocks on the SMs.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: In an inference server: double buffering and reading the gaps
question: In Nsight Systems, the CPU thread sits inside cudaMemcpyAsync for the full 4 ms that the H2D row shows a copy, and the kernel row is empty during those 4 ms. What does this signature point to?
options: Launch overhead: too many small kernels
A CUDA graph that was invalidated during capture
Two streams competing for one copy engine
A pageable host buffer: the copy fell back to synchronous behaviour, so the CPU could not move on
explain: A truly asynchronous copy returns at once, and the CPU thread moves on while the copy engine works. Blocking for the whole transfer is the pageable fallback from lesson 2. Launch-bound traces show many tiny kernels with the CPU busy issuing them, and a contended copy engine still leaves the CPU free.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: Which statement about what a cross-encoder outputs is correct?
options: A query embedding and a document embedding that are compared with cosine
A ranked list of document ids from its own index
One relevance score per (query, document) pair
A probability distribution over the whole vocabulary for each document token
explain: A reranker such as monoBERT or bge-reranker (an open reranker family from BAAI, the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) returns a single number per pair. Ranking comes from sorting candidates by that number; there is no embedding and no index inside the model.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
question: Your budget for reranking is 60 ms per query on one GPU. With the model card's V100 numbers and the k / T model, which configuration fits?
options: MiniLM-L12-v2 over 100 candidates
MiniLM-L6-v2 over 100 candidates
BERT-large over 30 candidates
MiniLM-L6-v2 over 200 candidates
explain: MiniLM-L6-v2 needs 100 / 1800 s = 55.6 ms for 100 pairs. L12 needs 104.2 ms, BERT-large needs 300 ms for 30, and L6 over 200 needs 111 ms. Real overheads (tokenization, transfer) also count, so leave headroom.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
question: Which operation fits "I need to check later that this downloaded file has not changed, and secrecy does not matter"?
options: Hashing
Encoding
Encryption
Compression
explain: A hash gives a short fingerprint that changes if the file changes. (Lesson 9 adds the caveat: an attacker who can also replace the published hash needs a signature to stop them.)

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
question: Why is the user id passed as associated data instead of being encrypted with the message?
options: The server needs to read it to route the message, but it must still be bound to the ciphertext so it cannot be swapped
Associated data is encrypted twice
Associated data makes the ciphertext shorter
It lets the server skip tag verification
explain: Associated data stays readable but is covered by the tag. Changing it (for example to another user's id) makes decryption fail, as the code shows.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
question: You have a 32-byte random shared secret from a key exchange and need an encryption key and a MAC key. Which tool fits?
options: HKDF with two different info labels
Argon2id with high memory
SHA-1 of the secret, split in half
Use the secret directly for both
explain: The input is already high-entropy, so no stretching is needed. HKDF extracts and expands it into independent keys per label.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall
question: What was the root cause of CurveBall?
options: Certificate validation matched the public key without checking the curve parameters it belonged to
SHA-1 collisions in certificates
A weak random number generator in Windows
ECDSA nonce reuse by Microsoft
explain: A public key only means something together with its curve and generator. Accepting attacker-chosen parameters let the attacker choose a generator for which they knew the private key.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Padding oracles: when an error message decrypts your data
question: Why did Microsoft's MS10-070 fix work, where the custom-error workaround only made the attack harder?
options: It added a signature (MAC) over encrypted data, so modified ciphertexts are rejected before padding is examined
It switched ASP.NET from AES to Triple DES
It added a random delay to every error page
It encrypted the error messages
explain: Microsoft described the fix as additionally signing all data encrypted by ASP.NET. Once modified ciphertexts fail an integrity check first, there is no padding answer to observe. Uniform errors and random delays reduce the signal but do not remove it.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Signature nonces: reuse, weak randomness and deterministic signing
question: In the 2013 Android case, what did wallet users have to do after updating their apps?
options: Nothing, the update fixed old signatures
Change their wallet password
Move funds to new keys generated with the repaired random generator
Re-sign their old transactions
explain: Keys or signatures made with the broken generator stayed weak after the patch. Bitcoin.org told users to rotate: generate a new address with a repaired generator and send the funds there. Passwords and re-signing do not fix exposed keys.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
question: Your API gateway is fully patched, never speaks SSLv2, and still offers TLS 1.2 RSA key exchange for legacy clients. Its recorded sessions can still be at DROWN-style risk if which is true?
options: The gateway uses ECDSA certificates
Clients use HTTP/2
The gateway enables session resumption
Another server that still accepts SSLv2 holds the same RSA key
explain: DROWN is cross-protocol: the oracle can be any SSLv2 server holding the same key, even a mail server. Sessions that used RSA key exchange with the gateway become decryptable. Certificate type, HTTP/2 and resumption are unrelated. Remove SSLv2 everywhere and stop sharing keys.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
question: Why did the Court mention 'damage' and 'loss' when reading the statute?
options: Both focus on technological harms to data and systems, which fits a law aimed at hacking, not at misuse of information people may legitimately see
They prove Van Buren caused USD 5,000 of loss
They define the purpose test the government wanted
They only apply to civil cases, so they are irrelevant
explain: The opinion reasons from the statute's structure: the civil remedy's definitions of damage and loss address technological harm, which would be 'ill fitted' to remedying misuse of information employees permissibly access.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
question: Why is a sinkhole log sensitive even though it only contains infected machines' IP addresses?
options: IP addresses are encrypted keys
It identifies victims, who can be located and exploited by others before they clean up
It contains the malware's source code
It is not sensitive at all
explain: A list of infected addresses is a list of vulnerable, compromised machines. Shared with network owners and CERTs it speeds clean-up; published openly it is a target list. It is also personal data under laws such as the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, the EU's data protection law).

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
question: In the hash-chained log, why does editing entry 1 also break entry 2's seal?
options: Because entry 2's seal is computed over entry 2 plus entry 1's seal
Because SHA-256 is slow
Because entry 2 was also edited
Because JSON sorting changed
explain: Each seal includes the previous seal. Change any entry and its seal changes, which changes the input to every later seal. Only rewriting all later seals hides the edit, which is why seals must be stored out of the editor's reach.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: A team doubles the weight of Wikipedia in a fixed 100B-token run. What must also happen?
options: Other domains must lose weight, because the weights sum to 1 and the token budget is fixed
Nothing else changes, because Wikipedia is a small domain
The run must be extended so the other domains keep their token counts
The tokenizer must be retrained for the new mixture
explain: Domain weights are a probability vector over a fixed budget. Raising one weight necessarily lowers others, so every reweighting is a trade, and the interesting question is whether a trade can help everything (lesson 4 shows it can).

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
question: DoReMi assigns 5 percent to a domain with 1B unique tokens, and you plan a 2T-token run. What happens, and what should you do?
options: Nothing: 5 percent is a small weight, so the domain cannot be over-read
The domain is read 10 times, which is fine because repeated data is as good as new
The domain is read 100 times, worth about 16 fresh passes by Muennighoff et al.'s fit; cap it near 4 epochs (weight 0.002) and give the rest to domains with unique data left
Drop the domain, because any repetition hurts the model
explain: 0.05 x 2T = 100B tokens from a 1B-token domain: 100 epochs. The fit gives an effective size of about 16.4 units for 100 read, so most of that compute is wasted. Capping at 4 epochs keeps 4B tokens (weight 0.002). Some repetition is fine, so dropping the domain throws away useful data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
question: Two pages share 85 percent of their shingles (Jaccard 0.85). Their MinHash signatures are split into 20 bands of 5 hashes; a pair becomes a candidate if all 5 minimums agree in at least one band. How likely is it that they are compared?
options: About 44 percent, the chance one band matches
About 85 percent, the Jaccard similarity itself
About 5 percent
Over 99.99 percent
explain: One band matches with probability 0.85 to the 5th = 0.444. All 20 bands miss with probability (1 - 0.444) to the 20th, about 8 in a million, so the pair is compared with probability 1 - 0.000008, over 99.99 percent. Banding turns a moderate per-band chance into near certainty for very similar pairs.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
question: You vectorize `sum += pts[i].x` over AoS `Point {float x, y, z;}` with 8-wide AVX. What does the ISPC guide say the compiler must do to load eight x values?
options: A gather (or one scalar load per lane on CPUs without gather), because the x values are 12 bytes apart
One aligned 32-byte vector load
Nothing special: the cache line already holds all eight x values
Convert the array to SoA automatically at compile time
explain: The x values sit at offsets 0, 12, ..., 84, not adjacent, so a single contiguous load cannot fill the register. The guide says such an access "accesses non-sequential memory locations", so a gather is required. They also span 2 cache lines, not 1.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
question: In the Pegasus case, which finding shows the bucket held more than personal data?
options: It contained over 1.6 million crew files
It was open from February 2022
It was fixed three weeks after notification
Its source code contained plain-text passwords and secret keys, which could unlock other systems
explain: Credentials in a leaked bucket extend the exposure beyond the bucket itself: SafetyDetectives warned the keys could let someone tamper with flight data. Personal data and dates matter, but they do not show the leak reaching other systems.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Encryption at rest, layer by layer: disk, database, field
question: Why bind the row id and column name as associated data when encrypting a field?
options: It makes the ciphertext shorter
It hides the row id
Decryption fails if an encrypted value is moved to another row or column, so swaps are detected
It removes the need for a nonce
explain: Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Decrypting with different associated data raises InvalidTag, as the demo shows. It does not hide or shorten anything, and AES-GCM still needs a unique nonce per encryption.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
question: What does exact data match add over a pattern-based SSN detector?
options: It finds SSNs in images
It encrypts the SSN before sending
It confirms the number is one of your own records (via salted hashes) and can check for matching fields from the same row nearby
It removes the need for a pattern
explain: EDM compares hashes of found values against hashes of your table, and then looks for secondary fields from the same record, which cuts false positives sharply. It still needs a pattern-based type to find the primary element first.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Disposal as a process: Morgan Stanley's drives and the certificate
question: A vendor returns a PDF titled 'Certificate of Destruction' listing a batch number but no serial numbers or method. What should the asset owner do?
options: Accept it: the title says destruction
File it and close the ticket
Reject it until it lists each device's serial number, the sanitisation method and technique, and who verified it, then reconcile against the inventory
Ask the vendor to add a company logo
explain: A certificate is only evidence if it can be matched device by device to the inventory and says what was done and by whom (SP 800-88 Rev. 2's list). In Morgan Stanley's case, documents that were not certificates of destruction at all went unreviewed.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Build a low-interaction honeypot on localhost
question: Why does the lab bind the honeypot to 127.0.0.1 and not 0.0.0.0?
options: 127.0.0.1 is faster
Binding to 0.0.0.0 is not allowed in Python
Only loopback is reachable from this machine alone; 0.0.0.0 would expose the listener on every network interface
127.0.0.1 hides the honeypot from the operating system
explain: 0.0.0.0 means all interfaces, including your Wi-Fi or office LAN. A lab honeypot should only be reachable by the test client on the same machine.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honey records and honeywords: decoys inside your data
question: Why must the honeychecker be a separate system from the login server?
options: So that stealing the login server's hash file does not also reveal which sweetword is real
Because PBKDF2 needs its own server
To make logins faster
Because honeywords are stored in plaintext
explain: If the index lived next to the hashes, the thief would steal both and know the real password. Juels and Rivest suggest running the two in separate administrative domains.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Legal, ethical and safety limits of deception
question: Which control most directly addresses the risk that a high-interaction honeypot is used to attack other networks?
options: A login banner
Outbound containment (data control) at a gateway in front of the decoy
A longer log retention period
Naming the decoy like a production server
explain: Banners address consent for monitoring and naming addresses believability. Only egress containment stops the decoy from being used against third parties.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Building batch-invariant kernels: RMSNorm, matmul and attention
question: A kernel always uses exactly 4 split-KV pieces, spread evenly over the keys in the launch. Token 600 of a prompt is computed once inside a 1000-token prefill chunk and once on its own in decode. Why can its output bits differ?
options: They cannot: the number of splits is fixed, so the reduction is identical.
Decode uses a different softmax formula from prefill.
The KV cache stores keys at lower precision than the prefill path.
Even splits put boundaries at 250 and 500 inside the 1000-key chunk but at 150, 300 and 450 for 600 keys alone; a fixed size of 256 puts them at 256 and 512 both times.
explain: A fixed count still places the boundaries relative to the extent of the launch, and that extent depends on how many query tokens are processed together. A fixed split size places them at multiples of the size from position 0, so the same token always sees the same tree. Nothing in the question involves precision or a different formula.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Why it matters: true on-policy RL and reproducible evaluation
question: Your RL sampler and trainer differ by small, frequent logit gaps (KL near 1e-3) on a dense model. When is importance weighting a sufficient fix, and when would you pay for bitwise equality?
options: Importance weighting is never sufficient; any nonzero KL eventually collapses training.
Bitwise equality is only needed for MoE models; dense models never need it.
Weighting suffices while gaps are small and corrected every step, as in the Thinking Machines run; pay for bitwise equality when large-gap tokens are common or you need a strict on-policy baseline.
Neither: lowering the learning rate removes the off-policy bias.
explain: The importance-weighted run trained smoothly at KL near 0.001, so weighting can be enough. Its weak spot is the rare token with a large gap, which MoE routing makes frequent, and any study of off-policy effects needs a true on-policy reference. Bitwise equality makes the off-policy term zero. A smaller learning rate shrinks the step but does not remove the bias.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness
question: Your DST suite injects only crashes that always restart within 2 simulated seconds and partitions that always heal within 5. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
options: Two leaders committing different values in the same term
A follower that never catches up while one peer stays permanently down
A torn write corrupting the log
An off-by-one in log index comparison
explain: That is a liveness bug, and it hides whenever faults heal on their own, exactly as in TigerBeetle's resonance bug. The other options are safety violations that can show up under transient faults. To catch liveness bugs, make some faults permanent and require a healthy quorum to keep making progress.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Runners: where pipeline code runs, and how to isolate it
question: A team runs self-hosted runners and adds a script that wipes and re-images each VM after a job finishes. GitHub's guidance says this is weaker than it looks. Why?
options: Re-imaging is too slow to matter
GitHub-hosted runners are never wiped either
Wiping removes the runner's registration token, which breaks the next job
Nothing guarantees the runner took only one job before the wipe, so a second job (possibly privileged) can still land on a dirty machine; JIT runners are registered for exactly one job
explain: The secure use reference says automatic destruction might not be as effective as intended because there is no way to guarantee a self-hosted runner only runs one job. A just-in-time runner is removed by GitHub after at most one job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
question: A pull_request_target workflow checks out PR code but has a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets. Before GitHub's cache restrictions, what could still go wrong?
options: The PR code could use the job's cache token to write cache entries under main's scope, which a later release workflow would restore
Nothing: a read-only token cannot change anything
The PR could merge itself
The runner would crash
explain: This is exactly Adnan Khan's finding: the runtime cache token is separate from GITHUB_TOKEN. Writing into main's cache scope turned a low-privilege job into code inside the release.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Policy as code with OPA and Rego
question: In Rego, a rule body has five lines. Four are true for a resource and one is false. What happens?
options: The rule does not fire for that resource, because lines in a body are joined by AND
The rule fires, since most lines are true
Rego raises an error
The rule fires once for each true line
explain: All lines in a body must hold for the same choice of variables. To express OR, write a second rule with the same name.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: Which of these is still a gap in the finished pipeline, and needs a different control?
options: A PR that edits the Makefile to steal secrets
An engineer opening a port in the console during an incident
A tampered pip cache restored by the release job
A wildcard OIDC trust on the apply role
explain: The first, third and fourth are handled inside the pipeline (no secrets on PRs, no release caches, an exact environment trust checked by policy). Console changes skip the pipeline; drift detection, and cloud guardrails that limit who may change security groups, are the controls for them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
question: A learner trains the diffusion model but forgets change 3, keeping the AR loader whose targets are the inputs shifted by one. Attention is bidirectional. What does training do?
options: It works the same, since the shift does not matter
Wherever the next character is visible the model just copies it, so the loss falls without real learning, and outputs no longer predict their own positions as the sampler expects
Training fails with a shape error
It becomes an ordinary autoregressive model
explain: With full attention and a target of x[i+1] at position i, the answer sits in the input one position to the right whenever that position is visible. The model learns to copy its neighbour. Causal attention is what makes the shifted target a real prediction task. DiffuLLaMA's shift in lesson 8 is different: output i is scored only when position i+1 itself is masked, so nothing leaks.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU
question: Which metric does a chat user notice first if prefills are always scheduled ahead of decodes on a busy colocated GPU?
options: Neither, since prefill priority helps everyone
Throughput in tokens per second must drop
TTFT gets worse
TPOT/TBT gets worse: running streams stutter while new prompts are processed
explain: Prioritizing prefill keeps TTFT low but every prefill iteration delays the next token of every running request. Splitwise notes that letting a waiting prompt preempt token generation shortens TTFT but can substantially increase the tail of TBT. Throughput may even rise; latency of the other phase is what suffers.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: The KV handoff in detail: protocol, layouts and failures
question: Prefill runs TP=4 and decode TP=2 for a model with 8 KV heads and head-major KV blocks. For a 128-block request, how many block reads does each decode rank issue?
options: 128, one per block, as with equal TP
256: each D rank needs 4 heads held by 2 P ranks, so 2 reads per block
512: every D rank reads every P rank
64, because a D block holds two P blocks
explain: A D rank's 4 heads are split over 2 P ranks (2 heads each), so it reads 2 slices per block: 2 x 128 = 256. Reading every P rank would fetch heads the D rank does not own; block counts do not change with TP, only the heads per block slice.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: From sectors to partitions to image files
question: An MBR shows exactly one partition, type 0xEE, covering the whole disk. What should your tool do next?
options: Report a single unformatted partition
Read the GPT header at LBA 1 and its partition entries; the MBR is only a protective placeholder
Treat the disk as wiped, since 0xEE marks erased space
Search for 0x55 0xAA signatures to find hidden MBRs
explain: Type 0xEE is the GPT protective MBR. The real partition table is the GPT starting at LBA 1 (signature EFI PART). It does not mean unformatted or wiped.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The USN change journal: a diary of every file change
question: The oldest record in a server's change journal is from three days ago. Your intrusion window starts two weeks ago. What do you write?
options: No files were changed before three days ago
The intruder deleted the journal
The journal does not cover the window; absence of earlier records says nothing about earlier activity
The server was rebuilt three days ago
explain: The journal is trimmed from the start once it exceeds its maximum size, so on a busy volume coverage is short. Deletion or a rebuild would need other evidence (for example a USN reset or a process event).

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
question: A registry key's last write time is 2026-03-02 14:28. Which statement is safe?
options: Every value under this key was written at 14:28
A user opened this key in regedit at 14:28
The key or at least one of its values was last modified at 14:28
The key was created at 14:28
explain: Microsoft defines it as the last time the key or any of its values was modified. It is per key, not per value, and it records modification, not viewing or creation.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Live acquisition and encryption: the Ross Ulbricht laptop (2013)
question: A live acquisition inevitably changes the running system. Which ACPO principle governs this?
options: Principle 1: no action should change data that may be relied on in court, so live acquisition is forbidden
Principle 3: only a second examiner may access live systems
Principle 4: the investigation lead must perform the acquisition
Principle 2: the person accessing original data must be competent and able to explain the relevance and implications of their actions
explain: Principle 2 covers the case where accessing original data is necessary. Principle 1 is the default, not a ban; Principle 3 requires an audit trail; Principle 4 puts overall responsibility on the person in charge.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Filtered-DiskANN: label-aware Vamana graphs
question: A marketplace adds thousands of new listings an hour, each tagged with 1 to 5 of about 800 category labels, and queries filter by one category. Which Filtered-DiskANN build fits?
options: StitchedVamana, rebuilt nightly
A separate Vamana index per category
Plain Vamana with post-filtering
FilteredVamana, which builds incrementally and applies its label rule locally, so new points can be inserted
explain: The paper notes FilteredVamana suits dynamic growth because its label rule only involves a node's own neighbors. StitchedVamana searches faster but is built from per-label graphs at once, and inserts risk breaking that structure. Per-label indexes multiply storage when points carry several labels; post-filtering fails for rare categories.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
question: At step 0 the policy equals the reference. What is the DPO loss of every pair, and what is each pair's gradient weight?
options: Loss 0 and weight 0, since nothing has changed
Loss 1 and weight 1
It depends on how strongly the reference prefers y_w
Loss ln 2 (about 0.693) and weight 0.5
explain: All log-ratios are 0, so the margin is 0 for every pair regardless of the reference's own preference. $-\log \sigma(0) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ and the weight is $\sigma(0) = 0.5$. The reference's preference cancels because DPO only scores improvement over the reference.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
question: Why does KTO estimate $z_0$ from mismatched (prompt, other example's output) pairs instead of each example's own output?
options: Because own outputs are usually chosen to be clearly good or bad, so their rewards are unrepresentatively large
Because mismatched pairs need no forward pass
Because the own output's log-ratio is always zero
Because it makes the estimate unbiased
explain: The paper says matched outputs have often been deliberately picked as canonically good or bad, giving high-magnitude rewards that would skew the reference point. The mismatched estimate still costs an extra forward pass and is explicitly biased (clamping adds upward bias), but it is cheap and stable.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
question: Which step is the real point of no return, where undoing it needs more than flipping a flag back?
options: Starting dual writes
Switching reads to the new store
Switching writes to the new store while still archiving to the old one
Stopping writes to the old store and deleting its data
explain: As long as some code keeps the old store current (dual writes in phases 1 to 3, archiving in phase 3), you can point traffic back at it. Once old writes stop and its data is deleted, going back would mean a new migration in the other direction.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
question: A gh-ost migration's applier is 6,000 events behind and applies 10,000 events per second. Using the simplified model, roughly how long are writes blocked during cut-over?
options: About 6 ms
About 60 ms
About 600 ms
About 6 seconds
explain: 6,000 events at 10,000 events per second take 0.6 s. That is why tools throttle and wait for lag to be small before cutting over: the write pause grows with the backlog.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: PQXDH: a post-quantum first message, and what formal analysis found
question: An adversary records PQXDH traffic in 2026 and gets a large quantum computer in 2040. The one-time KEM prekey was deleted. What can they read?
options: Not the SK: they would also need to break ML-KEM/Kyber or have stolen the deleted KEM private key
Everything, because X25519 is broken
Only the first message
Everything, because the signature is XEdDSA
explain: SK mixes the DH values and SS. A quantum computer recovers the DH values but SS needs the KEM private key, deleted after use. The spec states that recorded sessions stay safe in this case.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Post-quantum ratcheting: Signal's SPQR and iMessage PQ3
question: Why does SPQR spread a KEM exchange across messages with erasure codes rather than just splitting it into fixed pieces?
options: To compress the data
Because ML-KEM requires it
So any sufficient set of chunks rebuilds it, and a middleman dropping one specific chunk cannot stall the exchange
To hide message lengths
explain: With fixed pieces, losing piece 3 forever blocks completion. Erasure-coded chunks are interchangeable; the blog notes this covers messages dropped by a malicious middleman too.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Group chats: pairwise fan-out, sender keys, and who decides membership
question: In the vulnerable toy, which party really controls the group's confidentiality?
options: The group admin
The server, because clients send keys to whatever member list it provides
Mallory
Nobody
explain: Whoever decides the recipient list of the sender key decides who can read. If that list is unauthenticated server data, the server holds the power E2EE was meant to remove.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Backups and cloud copies: the quiet way around E2EE
question: A design wraps the backup key with scrypt(PIN) and stores the wrapped key on the provider's server. What is the core weakness?
options: scrypt is broken
The backup is too large
AES cannot wrap keys
A short PIN can be guessed offline by anyone holding the wrapped key; nothing limits attempts
explain: A slow KDF only raises the cost per guess; 10,000 PINs is still tiny. An HSM or secure element that counts failures (as in WhatsApp's vault) or a long random key held by the user removes offline guessing.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Lawful access and client-side scanning
question: Why does a NeuralHash-style perceptual hash behave differently from SHA-256 for this purpose?
options: It is longer
It uses a key
It is designed so similar images collide, which makes deliberate collisions and evasions possible with small image changes
It is computed on the server
explain: A cryptographic hash changes completely on any change, so it only finds exact copies. A perceptual hash tolerates changes by design, and Struppek et al. showed slight changes can force or prevent matches.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
question: Which statement about the verifier is correct?
options: It checks programs at every execution, so bugs are caught at runtime
It only checks the first 4,096 instructions of a program
It lets tracing programs call any kernel function directly
It proves a program is safe for the kernel but does not judge whether the data it collects is sensitive
explain: Verification is a one-time load-time proof of safety, not a security policy. Access control is separate (root, or CAP_BPF plus CAP_PERFMON for tracing). Since v5.2 the complexity limit is 1M processed instructions, and programs call a fixed set of helpers rather than arbitrary functions.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
question: Two candidate models have the same parameter count. Model B has half the multiply-adds but twice the peak activation size. On a battery sensor with very little SRAM, which statement is right?
options: B is always better because it does less arithmetic
Parameter count alone decides, so they are equivalent
B may not run at all, because peak activation memory is a separate hard limit
A is always better because activations dominate energy
explain: Parameters, multiply-adds and peak activation memory are three independent budgets. If B's peak activations exceed the arena, it cannot run no matter how few operations it has.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: After magnitude pruning 50% of weights, the exported LiteRT file is exactly as large as before. What happened?
options: Pruning failed and should be repeated with a higher threshold
The zeros are still stored densely; you need compression or a sparse format to see savings
int8 quantization undid the pruning
LiteRT does not support models with zero weights
explain: A pruned dense tensor still stores every zero. The LiteRT docs say pruned models are the same size on disk and only compress better. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once well over half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Citrix Bleed, 2023: a length bug that leaked logged-in sessions
question: snprintf(buf, 40, ...) returns 56. What does 56 mean?
options: 56 bytes were written into buf, overflowing it
It is an error code
The full output would have been 56 bytes; only 39 characters and a terminating zero were written
It is the address of the buffer
explain: snprintf truncates safely but reports the length it would have needed. Using that number as a send length is the bug; comparing it with the buffer size is the fix.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: The patch race: KEV-driven deadlines for edge devices
question: Under BOD 26-04, moving a FortiOS device with CVE-2018-13379 off the internet changes its deadline from 3 to 14 days. Why does Citrix Bleed stay at 3 days and forensic triage when internal?
options: Citrix Bleed is older
Internal assets are never exempt
CISA rates Citrix Bleed automatable with total control, and that row (row 9) stays at 3 days and triage even when not exposed
Because NetScaler is a load balancer
explain: The table keeps the strictest deadline for exploited bugs that are automatable and give total control, whatever the exposure. The FortiOS read is rated partial control, so its internal row is 14 days.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: End of support, hardening and the replace decision
question: An internet-facing firewall reached end of support last month. A new KEV entry covers its product line. What is the right plan?
options: Wait for the vendor's patch
Rely on the IPS signature forever
Lower its CVSS score in the scanner
Treat it as a replacement now: isolate or restrict it as a stop-gap, check it for compromise, and decommission it
explain: No patch will come after EOS. Stop-gaps (blocking exposure, signatures) buy time while it is replaced. BOD 26-02 sets the same direction for federal agencies, and ED 25-03 ordered EOS ASA models disconnected.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: In a GRPO group, all 8 sampled responses are correct but their lengths differ. With correctness reward only, what is the policy gradient signal from this group?
options: Zero: every reward is equal, so every advantage is 0, and length gets no push either way
Strongly favors the shortest response
Strongly favors the longest response
Negative for all responses, since the mean is subtracted
explain: Equal rewards give zero advantages, so the group teaches nothing. Kimi's length reward breaks the tie inside such groups, which is exactly where length can be cut without hurting accuracy.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
question: Same paper, 7B model, MATH500 (accuracy %, mean tokens): Thinking 90.2 at 3,674; NoThinking 80.6 at 697; DPO-shortest 91.6 at 2,499; Arora-Zanette 91.8 at 2,899; AdaptThink 92.0 at 1,875. Which configurations form the Pareto frontier?
options: Thinking and AdaptThink
Arora-Zanette and DPO-shortest
All five: each is best at something
NoThinking and AdaptThink
explain: AdaptThink is the most accurate and cheaper than everything except NoThinking, so it dominates Thinking, DPO-shortest and Arora-Zanette. NoThinking is the only cheaper point. Note that 92.0 vs 91.8 is well inside the noise on 500 problems: the frontier claim rests on tokens, not on that accuracy gap.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: HTML character references and the order a browser decodes
question: Why should the scheme check run on the plain-text URL and not on the HTML you are about to output?
options: Plain text is shorter, so the check is faster
The plain-text value is what the browser's URL parser will see once it undoes your HTML encoding
Browsers ignore schemes in encoded HTML
HTML encoding removes the scheme
explain: Your attribute encoding is undone exactly once by the browser's HTML parser. Checking the plain value and then encoding it means the URL parser sees the same string your check approved.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577
question: Which change removes this whole class of bug from a Windows program, rather than patching one character?
options: Add U+00AD to a blocklist
Use the wide (W) APIs and UTF-8 end to end so no lossy ANSI conversion happens
Upper-case all arguments before checking
Escape arguments twice
explain: Blocklists miss the next mapped character (yen sign, fullwidth quote, and more across many code pages). Removing the lossy conversion removes the second meaning.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: URL parser differentials: one URL, two hosts
question: What is the core of Orange Tsai's application-level mitigation for SSRF parser differentials?
options: Use a longer blocklist of internal IP ranges
Parse the URL once, validate the parsed host or IP, and build the request from those parts instead of reusing the raw input
Percent-decode the URL twice before checking
Only allow URLs shorter than 100 characters
explain: If the component that fetches never re-parses the original string, there is no second interpretation to disagree with. Blocklists and length limits do not address the differential.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
question: Which pairing of bug and design fix from this course is correct?
options: Spotify takeover: switch to bcrypt password hashing
CouchDB roles: reject duplicate JSON keys before any component acts on the document
Trojan Source: normalise source files with NFKC
PHP CVE-2024-4577: add a CSP header
explain: CouchDB's bug was two parsers disagreeing on duplicate keys. Spotify needed an idempotent canonicalisation, Trojan Source needs bidi controls rejected or made visible (NFKC leaves them alone), and the PHP bug needs no lossy ANSI conversion before argument parsing.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: AMSI in depth: what the scanner sees, and what it cannot
question: A script is downloaded as text, decoded twice in memory (Base64 then XOR) and run by PowerShell. Which content does AMSI receive?
options: The original downloaded text, exactly as it was on the wire
Only the file name of the script
Nothing: AMSI only scans files saved to disk
The decoded code PowerShell is about to run, after both layers are removed
explain: PowerShell calls AMSI with the code it is about to execute, after de-obfuscation. That is the design point: obfuscation must be undone before the engine can run the code, so the scan sees plain code.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: WMI: remote execution, event subscriptions and their telemetry
question: WMIC has been removed from your Windows 11 24H2 fleet. Does that remove WMI as a lateral movement channel?
options: Yes, WMI no longer works without WMIC
No: only the command-line tool is gone; WMI itself, reachable through PowerShell CIM cmdlets and other clients over DCOM or WinRM, is unchanged
Yes, because DCOM was removed at the same time
No, but WMI now only works locally
explain: Microsoft is explicit that the deprecation and removal apply only to the WMIC command-line utility and that WMI itself is not affected. Detection must still watch WmiPrvSE child processes and remote DCOM and WinRM traffic.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Credential hardening: LAPS, LSA protection and Credential Guard
question: A new Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise laptop joins the domain and meets the hardware requirements. Nobody configured Credential Guard. What is its likely state?
options: Off, it must always be enabled manually
Running by default, without UEFI lock
Running with UEFI lock that cannot be removed
Running only for local accounts
explain: Microsoft documents default enablement on Windows 11 22H2 and later for domain-joined, licensed devices meeting the requirements, unless explicitly disabled, and notes the default is without UEFI lock so admins can disable it remotely.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: XDR, MDR and running EDR well: the HSE lesson
question: Your EDR flags Mimikatz on a finance workstation at 02:00. Which response best matches the lessons of this course?
options: Email the server team in the morning
Isolate the device (it stays connected to the EDR service), collect an investigation package, and treat the user's and any cached admin credentials as compromised
Uninstall the EDR to stop the alerts
Wait to see whether ransomware follows
explain: Credential theft is the step before lateral movement. Isolation cuts the attacker's network path while keeping the device observable; credentials exposed on that host must be reset. Waiting is how HSE lost eight weeks.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
question: A seq2point model for the fridge is trained with W = 599 at 6-second samples. Which input does it use to predict fridge power at time t?
options: Only the mains sample at time t
About an hour of mains before time t only
About an hour of mains centred on time t, past and future
The fridge's own past power readings
explain: 599 samples x 6 s is about 60 minutes in total, roughly 30 minutes on each side of the midpoint. Seq2point is non-causal: it uses both past and future mains. It never sees sub-metered fridge data at test time, only the aggregate.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
question: City has m = 0.90 and u = 0.05 for exact agreement. A new data source has many members who typed their home city instead of the company's HQ city, so true duplicates agree on city only 45% of the time. What happens to the exact-city weight?
options: It stays 4.17 because u did not change
It drops to log2(0.45/0.05) = 3.17
It becomes negative
It doubles, because more disagreement means more information
explain: m measures how often true matches agree. Halving m from 0.90 to 0.45 subtracts exactly 1 from log2(m/u). Disagreement also becomes less damning: the else weight rises from log2(0.10/0.95) = -3.25 to log2(0.55/0.95) = -0.79.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Evaluating entity resolution: labels, pairwise and cluster metrics
question: A model change raises pairwise F1 from 0.90 to 0.99 but lowers B-cubed F1 from 0.93 to 0.92. What most likely happened?
options: The labels were corrupted
Precision improved and recall stayed the same
Pairwise F1 and B-cubed always move in opposite directions
It merged or repaired a few large clusters (many pairs) while breaking many small entities (few pairs each)
explain: Pairwise metrics weigh an entity by its number of pairs, which grows with the square of its size; B-cubed weighs every record once. Gains on a few big entities can outweigh losses on many small ones only in the pairwise view, exactly as in the 90 + 10 versus 20-pairs example.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
question: Why do Microsoft 365 services not need to see a user's password?
options: They store a copy of each password hash
They use Kerberos tickets from the on-premises domain
They trust tokens signed by the tenant's Entra ID, which did the authentication
They ask the user's device for a certificate on every request
explain: Exchange, SharePoint and Teams are relying parties: they validate a token Entra ID signed for them. That is why a stolen or forged token is as good as a login, the theme of lessons 6 to 9.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
question: Which single control from Microsoft's guidance would most directly have limited the damage of step 4?
options: Blocking all residential IP addresses
Requiring users to change passwords every 30 days
Scoping mailbox access for apps with RBAC for applications in Exchange Online, and removing unneeded full_access_as_app grants
Disabling Teams
explain: full_access_as_app opens every mailbox through EWS. Removing it where unneeded, and using RBAC for applications to restrict an app to the mailboxes it really needs, caps what a hijacked or malicious app can read. IP blocking fails against residential proxies.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
question: Which log should an analyst check first for silent use of a stolen refresh token?
options: Interactive sign-ins, filtered on failed MFA
The Windows Security log on the domain controller
Non-interactive user sign-ins from IPs or devices the user never used interactively
Exchange message trace
explain: Redeeming a refresh token is a non-interactive sign-in. Microsoft's playbook calls out unfamiliar non-interactive sign-ins for immediate attention.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
question: MailItemsAccessed shows a Sync record from the attacker's IP for the Inbox folder. How should the investigator scope the exposure?
options: Only messages listed in Bind records are exposed
Nothing, because Sync is a background Outlook process
Assume all items in the synced scope were downloaded; Microsoft's guidance treats a sync in the attacker's context as the whole mailbox being compromised
Only messages read in the last 2 minutes
explain: Sync records are per folder, not per message, because a client downloads sets of items. Microsoft's forensic steps say that if a sync occurred in the attacker's context, assume they synced everything and the whole mailbox is compromised.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait
question: Why can epoll_wait cost O(ready) while poll costs O(watched)?
options: epoll uses a faster hash function for file descriptors
epoll caches socket data in user space
The kernel keeps the interest set between calls and a per-socket callback adds an item to the ready list when its state changes
epoll checks only the first 1024 descriptors
explain: poll is stateless: each call re-sends and re-scans everything. epoll is stateful: registration happens once with epoll_ctl, and readiness is pushed onto a ready list by a wait-queue callback at the moment it happens. epoll_wait only drains that list.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
question: A leaderboard shows exact scores to five decimals, allows 10 submissions a day, and has a 60-query public set. Which change most directly limits how much label information each submission leaks?
options: Raise the daily cap to 50 so teams stop hoarding submissions
Show a new score only when a submission beats the current best by a significance margin, otherwise repeat the old best
Switch the metric from nDCG@10 to MRR
Publish the per-query scores so teams can debug faster
explain: That is the Ladder idea. Most submissions then reveal nothing beyond "not a clear improvement", which caps what an adaptive analyst can learn about the hidden labels. More submissions or per-query scores leak more, and changing the metric does not change the leakage.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
question: Which statement best describes the purpose of an exploit mitigation?
options: To find memory bugs during testing
To translate C code into a memory-safe language
To make turning a bug into attacker control harder or less reliable, without fixing the bug
To stop all attacks against a process once enabled
explain: Finding bugs is the job of sanitizers and fuzzers; mitigations ship in production and assume bugs remain. They break links in the attack chain and raise the cost of an exploit, but none of them stops every attack.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why one leaked pointer defeats ASLR, and guessing at scale
question: A process has 28 bits of mmap randomness, but an attacker finds a bug that prints one pointer into libc. How many guesses do they now need to locate any function in libc?
options: About 2^27 on average
About 2^14
Essentially none: the leaked pointer plus fixed offsets inside libc gives every libc address
explain: Randomization shifts the whole library by one slide. Offsets inside it are fixed and public (anyone can read them from the same libc build). One leaked libc pointer reveals the slide and therefore every libc address.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Kernel mitigations: SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, KPTI and EternalBlue
question: A kernel bug lets an attacker make the kernel call a function pointer whose value they choose. With SMEP and SMAP enabled, why can't they simply point it at code in their own process?
options: Because KPTI unmaps user memory completely
Because user processes cannot contain executable code
Because SMEP makes the CPU fault when executing a user-space page in kernel mode
Because SMAP encrypts user memory
explain: SMEP blocks instruction fetches from user pages while in supervisor mode. The attacker must find code already in the kernel, which requires knowing kernel addresses: exactly what KASLR and leak prevention protect.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: With 64-byte lines, which pair of 8-byte variables can falsely share a line?
options: A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2038 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2010 and B at 0x2030
A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2080
explain: Divide by 64: 0x2010 and 0x2030 are both in line 0x80 (offsets 16 and 48). 0x2038 is in line 0x80 but 0x2040 starts line 0x81, so adjacent addresses can still be on different lines. Distance alone does not decide it; the line boundary does.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: A queue pads head and tail to 64 bytes each, yet still scales badly on x86-64. `perf c2c report --double-cl` shows heavy HITMs on one line pair: offset 0x0 written by `push` threads and 0x40 by `pop` threads. Likely cause?
options: True sharing on one variable
A compiler bug
False sharing caused by adjacent-line prefetching, since 0x0 and 0x40 are neighboring 64-byte lines
The two functions are on the same core
explain: Offsets 0x0 and 0x40 are 64 bytes apart, so with 64-byte lines they are different lines. When they still show up together, the adjacent-line (spatial) prefetcher pairing is the suspect; perf c2c's --double-cl option groups lines in pairs for exactly this. Padding to 128, as crossbeam and folly do on x86-64, is the usual fix.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt
question: Compared with FedAvg, which hyperparameter does FedAdam expose that FedAvg implicitly fixes at 1?
options: The client learning rate eta_l
The number of local epochs E
The server learning rate eta applied to the averaged client delta
The fraction of clients C sampled per round
explain: Written as FedOpt, FedAvg's server step is x plus 1 times the averaged delta. FedAdam replaces that with eta times m over (sqrt(v) + tau), adding beta_1, beta_2 and tau as well. The client learning rate, E and C exist in FedAvg already and keep their meaning.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model
